Newborn Care

Konar or sidr while breastfeeding: identity, claims and uncertain safety

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Konar, also called sidr in some settings, is a fruit name rather than a guarantee of one plant species or a safe breastfeeding remedy. Research does not establish that unidentified konar cleans breast milk or protects a baby from pollution. Food fruit and concentrated herbal products need separate consideration, with the actual plant, preparation and exposure checked.

First check which plant and preparation you mean

Konar and sidr can refer to different Ziziphus plants, including Ziziphus mauritiana and Ziziphus spina-christi. Chinese jujube, Ziziphus jujuba, is another species. Common names alone cannot establish identity, and results for one species, seed, leaf or extract cannot automatically be applied to another. These fruits are also different from frankincense, a Boswellia resin.

Many of these plants are thorny shrubs or trees with oval leaves, small flowers and fleshy fruit surrounding a hard stone. Colour, size, growth, harvest season and yield vary. Fruit may be eaten fresh or dried or made into preserves; wood, foliage and other parts also have non-food uses. None of those uses proves medicinal safety. Do not identify wild fruit from a photograph or assume a leaf, root or seed preparation is equivalent to edible flesh.

Traditional uses are not established treatment benefits

Claims include body or blood cleansing, improved circulation and oxygen delivery, more white blood cells, relief of headache, dizziness, stress, anxiety, irritability, anger or restlessness, and increased stamina. Other uses concern abdominal or back pain, gum swelling, lung or throat illness, cough and mucus, digestion, stomach ulcers and bladder stones. These are not established treatments for a breastfeeding parent.

Claims also include preventing osteoporosis, healing fractures, improving skin health or moisture, soothing skin irritation and reducing hair loss or promoting growth. Laboratory activity or a long tradition does not show clinical benefit, a safe dose or infant safety. Do not replace assessment and effective care for these problems with fruit, tea or an extract.

What does research say about cleaning breast milk?

A small 2016 randomized study enrolled 40 breastfeeding mothers in two groups; one group received Ziziphus jujuba fruit for eight weeks. It reported selected differences in milk lead and cadmium concentrations, but levels fell in both groups and there was no significant arsenic effect. This was a limited study of measured contaminants, not proof of improved infant health.

The findings do not establish a milk-detox treatment, a generally useful dose, or a benefit from a different plant sold as konar. They also do not establish increased milk supply or better nourishment. A study of a topical jujube product or a seed extract would answer a different question from eating unidentified fruit while nursing.

Suspected pollution exposure needs assessment, not a cleanse

For most infants, breastfeeding benefits outweigh the potential risks from environmental exposures, and reducing the exposure source matters. If you are worried about lead, chemicals at work, an unsafe product or another specific exposure, tell a clinician what happened. Testing and any temporary feeding plan depend on the substance and the parent’s and baby’s circumstances.

Do not start a fruit, herbal detox, fast or restrictive diet to purify milk. Do not automatically stop breastfeeding or discard milk because of a general pollution worry. Confirmed harmful exposure can require individual advice; lead assessment usually uses blood testing, not a home milk test or a fruit regimen.

Is food fruit different from a herbal remedy?

Yes. Edible flesh, strong tea, powdered leaves, roots, seeds, tinctures and concentrated extracts differ in their ingredients and exposure. A familiar food history does not establish a breastfeeding-safe amount for an uncertain species. No reports of harm is not the same as adequate safety research, and “moderation” is not a validated dose.

The NHS does not recommend herbal remedies during breastfeeding because safety cannot be guaranteed. Abu Dhabi’s health department also notes insufficient pregnancy and breastfeeding information for Ziziphus spina-christi fruit and advises avoidance in its English leaflet. That advice is not proof that every konar exposure is harmful. Discuss the correctly identified food or product individually rather than borrowing a dose or safety conclusion from another species.

Side-effect claims need careful interpretation

Seizures, tremor, memory or thinking problems are not established predictable consequences of eating ordinary konar fruit. Nor is there enough evidence to promise that a moderate amount has no adverse effects. Abdominal discomfort or bloating after food or a product deserves attention if persistent or substantial, but symptoms alone cannot identify the cause.

Product identity, other ingredients, contamination, medicines and underlying illness may matter. Stop further unsupervised medicinal use and seek advice if symptoms occur; keep the label. New neurological symptoms need medical assessment, and a first seizure, loss of consciousness or severe reaction needs emergency help rather than a home remedy.

Maternal gas does not pass through breast milk

The idea that a fruit’s “cold nature” or a parent’s bloating transfers gas into the baby’s milk is not an established explanation. Intestinal gas itself does not pass through breast milk. A baby crying after a feed does not prove that konar, or any one maternal food, caused it.

Check feeding and seek advice for persistent crying, poor growth or possible allergy rather than cutting out many foods or giving an infant herbal tea. Some babies have food-related conditions requiring an individual plan, but colic or fussiness alone is not proof. Do not give konar remedies, extracts or a homemade nipple preparation to a baby.

If you have already eaten fruit or taken a product

Record the common and botanical name if available, plant part, preparation, ingredients, amount and timing. Tell a pharmacist or clinician about medicines, symptoms, and your baby’s age, prematurity or jaundice history. A single exposure does not establish harm, and an unknown label needs clarification rather than a guess.

There is no universal evidence-based waiting time, milk-discard schedule or reason to wean after an unspecified konar exposure. Any feeding change should follow individual advice. Do not stop necessary prescribed medicines yourself, induce vomiting or try a detox; suspected poisoning needs prompt medical or poison-service advice.

Milk and feeding concerns need practical support

You do not need a special fruit to make good-quality milk. Aim for a varied diet and seek a feeding assessment if supply or milk transfer is a concern. A trained professional can observe attachment and swallowing and assess age-appropriate wet nappies, weight gain and possible illness or medicine effects.

Agree a feeding or expressing plan and follow-up. If extra milk is needed, use an individualized supplementation plan instead of delaying it for a fruit or herb trial. Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies or unusual drowsiness needs prompt assessment; do not wait for a product to work.

Warning symptoms must not wait

Seek emergency help for a first seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, breathing difficulty, or a possible severe allergic reaction with tongue or throat swelling, trouble swallowing, breathing symptoms or faintness. A rash is not required. Do not assume new symptoms are explained by fruit or a traditional property.

For a baby, breathing difficulty, blue, grey or unusually pale skin, a seizure, difficulty waking or unresponsiveness, or no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care. Poor feeding or other signs of dehydration need urgent assessment even without every warning sign. Tracking or checking a label must not delay care.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Check the plant name, part and preparation with a pharmacist or clinician before using konar as a remedy. Bring the label, medicine list and infant health details; do not borrow a dose from a different species.

Ask for a feeding assessment or specific exposure assessment when needed. Agree supplementation, testing and follow-up rather than trying to cleanse milk or automatically changing breastfeeding.

Stop further unsupervised medicinal use if symptoms occur and seek appropriate advice. Use emergency care for severe reactions or neurological symptoms and for a seriously unwell baby without waiting for every sign.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record feeds, wet nappies, product labels, medicines, symptoms and appointment questions. It cannot identify a plant, assess contamination, establish breastfeeding safety or diagnose low supply; warning symptoms and feeding difficulties need professional care.

When to seek help

Avoid using unidentified konar or concentrated herbal products as a breastfeeding remedy. No detox benefit or safe universal dose is established. Poor infant feeding, fewer wet nappies or unusual drowsiness needs prompt assessment. Infant breathing difficulty, blue/grey or unusually pale skin, a seizure, difficulty waking or no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care. A first seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a severe allergic reaction or breathing difficulty needs emergency help. Do not stop necessary prescribed medicines or change feeding automatically; suspected poisoning needs prompt medical advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A common name or photograph cannot confirm which konar or sidr species you have.
  • Limited jujube research does not establish a konar milk-detox treatment or infant protection.
  • Fruit and medicinal preparations differ; no universal breastfeeding-safe dose is established.
  • Review actual exposures and feeding concerns with a professional, and use emergency care for warning symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

Are the traditional benefits proven?

Claims about cleansing, circulation, blood cells, mood, pain, respiratory or digestive illness, bones, skin and hair are not established breastfeeding treatments. Traditional use and laboratory findings cannot establish a safe effective dose or infant safety.

Does too much konar cause seizures or memory damage?

These are not established predictable effects of ordinary fruit, and a safe threshold is not known. Do not dismiss new neurological symptoms or assume the fruit caused them. A first seizure or loss of consciousness needs emergency help.

Can konar remove toxins from breast milk?

A small study of Ziziphus jujuba measured some milk contaminants, with limited findings and no proof of infant health benefit. It does not establish detoxification by a different or unidentified konar product. Specific exposure concerns need clinical assessment.

Is konar safe while breastfeeding?

Species, plant part, preparation and exposure matter, and adequate breastfeeding safety information is lacking. Food use does not validate a safe dose. NHS advice does not recommend herbal remedies; ask about the actual product instead of assuming either guaranteed safety or certain harm.

Can my bloating give my baby gas through milk?

Intestinal gas does not pass through breast milk. Fussiness after a feed does not by itself diagnose a maternal food problem. Persistent crying, poor feeding, poor growth or suspected allergy needs individual assessment rather than broad food restrictions.

Should I discard milk after one exposure?

There is no universal waiting or milk-discard rule for an unspecified konar exposure. Keep the label and discuss amount, timing, medicines and infant health with a professional. Any temporary feeding plan should reflect the actual risk; one exposure does not prove harm.

What if I am worried about milk supply or pollution?

Arrange a feeding assessment for supply concerns and specific medical advice for a suspected chemical exposure. Necessary supplementation or exposure treatment should not be delayed for fruit, herbs or detox diets. Do not automatically stop breastfeeding or prescribed medicines yourself.

When is urgent or emergency help needed?

Poor infant feeding, fewer wet nappies or unusual drowsiness needs prompt assessment. A baby with breathing difficulty, blue/grey or unusually pale skin, a seizure, difficulty waking or no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care. A first seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a severe allergic reaction or breathing difficulty in an adult also needs emergency help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
